questions.q: Why does Northbridge Retail need centralized logging instead of reading log files on each server?
options: Local log files take up too much CPU
Autoscaled pods write their own logs and disappear when rescheduled, making per-host inspection impractical at scale
Centralized logging is required by law
Local logs can't use JSON formatting
questions.explain: With dozens of autoscaled, frequently rescheduled pods, there's no realistic way to SSH into every host — logs need to be shipped off and aggregated into one searchable system.

questions.q: In the ELK stack, what is Elasticsearch's role?
options: It's the web UI for building dashboards
It collects logs from each host and ships them onward
It's the distributed search engine that indexes the full content of every log line
It converts logs into metrics only
questions.explain: Elasticsearch is the indexing and search engine at the core of ELK. Logstash/Filebeat handle collection and shipping; Kibana is the UI on top.

questions.q: How does Grafana Loki's indexing approach differ from Elasticsearch's?
options: Loki indexes the full text of every log line, just like Elasticsearch
Loki indexes only a small set of labels and stores raw log text in cheap compressed chunks
Loki doesn't store logs at all, only metrics
Loki requires no query language
questions.explain: Loki is often described as 'Prometheus for logs' — it indexes labels like service and environment, keeping storage costs lower than full-text indexing, at the cost of slower broad text search.

questions.q: In the LogQL query `{service="checkout", environment="production"} |= "payment_timeout"`, what happens first?
options: A full-text search across every log line in the entire system
The query narrows to the checkout service's production logs using indexed labels, then text-searches within that already-narrow set
It deletes all non-matching log lines
It converts the logs into a Prometheus metric automatically
questions.explain: LogQL label selectors (the part in curly braces) use Loki's indexed labels to narrow the search cheaply before the `|=` text filter runs only against that smaller set of lines.

questions.q: Why might a team that already runs Prometheus and Grafana choose Loki over ELK for logging?
options: Loki is the only system that supports structured logs
Loki plugs into the same Grafana UI they already use, keeping metrics and logs in one place without a separate tool
ELK cannot be used with Kubernetes
Loki requires no storage at all
questions.explain: Teams already living in Grafana often add Loki so logs and metrics sit side by side in the same interface, avoiding context-switching to a separate Kibana instance.
